strengths: Clear motivation and clean architectural design: Disentangling semantic and acoustic modeling into two dedicated parallel streams directly tackles the inherent conflict between fine-grained acoustic reconstruction and high-level linguistic preservation in neural audio codecs.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper conducts extensive comparisons across speech reconstruction under both clean and noisy conditions (STOI, PESQ, UTMOS, SIM, WER), semantic probing on the ARCH benchmark, subjective MOS listening tests, and inference speed (RTF).

Rigorous speech disentanglement analysis: The evaluation of semantic-only and acoustic-only decoding modes (including WER, SIM, MSIM, and mel-spectrogram visualizations) convincingly demonstrates that speaker timbre and semantic content are cleanly decoupled.

Strong downstream validation: The proposed tokenizer is validated in a large-scale (100k-hour bilingual corpus) single-stage autoregressive TTS model with an interleaved flattening strategy, outperforming competitive pure AR baselines (Spark-TTS, Llasa) in WER/CER and UTMOS.
weaknesses: Incremental architectural novelty: The individual components (frozen pre-trained SSL/semantic tokenizer, neural codec encoder-decoder, auxiliary speaker verification loss, VQ-GAN training) are well-established paradigms in the recent speech codec literature (e.g., SemantiCodec, X-Codec, Mimi).

Heavy reliance on a pre-existing semantic tokenizer: The framework hinges entirely on a specific pre-trained speech tokenizer (Zeng et al., 2024b), restricting the end-to-end self-containment of the system and fundamentally bounding its applicability to speech rather than general audio/music.

Slight degradation in TTS speaker similarity: In the downstream TTS evaluation (Table 9), SAC exhibits lower speaker similarity (SIM) than baseline models (e.g., 0.54 vs. 0.58 for Spark-TTS on Seed-TTS test-en). While the authors attribute this to the lower token-rate variant (37.5 Hz), results with the 62.5 Hz configuration are missing to confirm this hypothesis.

Limited downstream SLM coverage: Despite claiming broad utility for speech language models and dialogue systems, downstream generative language modeling experiments are restricted strictly to TTS, leaving spoken dialogue or spoken language understanding LLMs unexamined.

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation spanning speech reconstruction (clean and noisy LibriSpeech), representation evaluation on the ARCH benchmark, downstream LLM-based TTS on a large-scale 100k-hour corpus, and subjective listening tests (MOS).

Strong empirical performance: SAC achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction naturalness (UTMOS > 4.25) and low WER at low bitrates (525 bps and 875 bps), outperforming strong recent baselines like WavTokenizer, BigCodec, and X-Codec2.

Convincing demonstration of token-level disentanglement: semantic-only decoding retains linguistic clarity while stripping speaker identity (SIM drops to 0.17 and collapses to a uniform voice), providing valuable properties for applications like voice anonymization.
Successful application to pure autoregressive (AR) TTS using a single-layer interleaved flattening strategy, achieving competitive WER/CER and high naturalness compared to Spark-TTS and Llasa.
weaknesses: Architectural novelty is relatively incremental: the framework essentially combines an existing pre-trained frozen semantic tokenizer (Zeng et al., 2024b) with an Encodec/DAC-style acoustic encoder and standard auxiliary losses.

Ablation results in Table 4 and Table 13 show that the auxiliary semantic supervision loss (Lsem) has negligible impact on reconstruction metrics and representation quality, suggesting this component adds minimal practical utility.

Downstream zero-shot TTS exhibits a noticeable drop in speaker similarity (SIM) compared to baselines like Spark-TTS (0.54 vs 0.58 on Seed-TTS English); while attributed to the lower token rate (37.5 Hz), no experimental comparison with the higher-rate variant is provided to verify this hypothesis.
The codec is limited to 16 kHz audio, whereas modern neural speech and audio codecs (e.g., DAC, BigCodec, CosyVoice) increasingly target 24 kHz or 44.1 kHz.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation covering multiple dimensions: speech reconstruction under both clean and noisy conditions, semantic probing on the ARCH benchmark, downstream zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) modeling, and runtime inference speed (RTF).

Strong performance on downstream zero-shot TTS: the authors integrate the dual-stream tokens into an autoregressive language model (Qwen3-0.6B) trained on 100k hours of speech using an interleaved flattening scheme, achieving high intelligibility (1.06% WER on English, 0.90% CER on Chinese) and strong naturalness.

Insightful speech disentanglement analysis: the paper presents quantitative (WER, SIM, MSIM) and qualitative (mel-spectrogram) evidence showing that decoding from semantic tokens alone retains linguistic content while normalizing speaker identity, whereas the acoustic stream alone retains pitch and harmonic contours without intelligible speech, indicating effective empirical separation.
Well-structured and thorough paper with extensive supplementary material, including human subjective MOS testing, data scaling ablations, and robustness evaluations under noisy conditions.
weaknesses: Limited architectural and conceptual novelty: the overall pipeline primarily combines pre-existing building blocks (a frozen pre-trained semantic tokenizer from GLM-4-Voice, an Encodec/DAC-style acoustic encoder, and an off-the-shelf ERes2Net speaker encoder) rather than introducing fundamentally new quantization or learning paradigms.

Heuristic disentanglement without explicit theoretical or structural constraints: while empirical disentanglement is observed, the acoustic encoder has no explicit bottleneck, mutual information minimization, or adversarial gradient reversal to prevent linguistic leakage; its specialization relies entirely on the presence of the frozen semantic stream and auxiliary speaker loss.

Discrepancy among objective reconstruction metrics: while UTMOS is notably high (even exceeding the ground truth, which often reflects GAN vocoder-style smoothing/enhancement artifacts), classic fidelity metrics such as PESQ-WB (2.59 at 875 bps, 2.18 at 525 bps) lag significantly behind established codecs like DAC (4.01 at 6 kbps) and BigCodec.

Incomplete repository details: the abstract ends with an unfinished sentence ('The code and pre-trained models are available at') without providing the repository URL or an anonymous repository link, hindering verification of reproducibility.

strengths: The dual-stream formulation cleanly separates semantic representation (via a frozen pre-trained semantic tokenizer) and acoustic modeling (via a neural codec stream), effectively addressing the optimization conflict observed in joint/distilled single-stream codecs.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across reconstruction metrics (STOI, PESQ, UTMOS, SIM, WER) under both clean (LibriSpeech test-clean) and noisy (LibriSpeech test-other) conditions, demonstrating competitive bitrates (525 bps and 875 bps) with strong intelligibility and speaker preservation.

Detailed evaluation on semantic representation benchmarks (ARCH) showing that SAC representations perform strongly across intent, digit, and emotion recognition tasks, outperforming several existing codecs and matching continuous SSL features.

Informative disentanglement experiments (Table 5 and Figure 3/4), showing that semantic-only reconstruction retains linguistic content while stripping speaker identity, and acoustic-only reconstruction preserves harmonic structure without intelligible linguistic content.
weaknesses: Lack of downstream generative validation: Although the paper heavily motivates SAC by its utility for Speech Language Models (SLMs) and Text-to-Speech (TTS), it does not evaluate SAC tokens in an actual downstream SLM, TTS, or voice conversion setup.

Reliance on automatic MOS (UTMOS) without subjective listening tests: SAC scores higher than the ground-truth audio on UTMOS (e.g., 4.25 vs. 4.09), which is a known artifact of neural MOS predictors favoring GAN-generated spectral details; formal human subjective evaluations (e.g., MUSHRA or crowd-sourced MOS) would be necessary to substantiate claims of superior perceptual quality.

Dependence on a strong pre-trained semantic tokenizer: The semantic modeling power originates substantially from the frozen external tokenizer of Zeng et al. (2024b), meaning the core semantic representation itself is not jointly learned or derived by SAC.

strengths: The paper presents a clear, well-motivated dual-stream architecture that decouples speech modeling into a frozen pre-trained semantic stream and a dedicated acoustic stream, effectively addressing the mutual interference often observed in joint semantic-acoustic codec training.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across reconstruction metrics (STOI, PESQ, UTMOS, SIM, WER) demonstrating competitive or superior performance at low bitrates (525 bps and 875 bps) compared to multiple strong baselines.

Strong evaluation of learned representations on the ARCH benchmark, showing that the decoupled tokens maintain strong semantic probing performance while acoustic tokens complement para-linguistic attributes (e.g., emotion).

Detailed disentanglement analysis (Table 5 and Figure 3/4) demonstrating that semantic-only reconstruction preserves linguistic intelligibility (low WER) while normalizing speaker identity, providing solid empirical evidence for token decoupling.
The paper is clearly written, logically structured, and provides good reproducibility details, including hyperparameter settings, dataset compositions, and planned open-sourcing.
weaknesses: The claimed suitability for generative speech language modeling (e.g., zero-shot TTS, voice conversion, or spoken dialogue) is not validated on actual generative downstream tasks; the evaluation is restricted to autoencoding/reconstruction and linear probing on classification tasks.

Perceptual audio quality is evaluated primarily via automated metrics (UTMOS and PESQ). Neural vocoders and GAN-based decoders can sometimes inflate neural MOS estimators; conducting formal subjective listening tests (e.g., MUSHRA or human MOS) would substantiate the perceptual quality claims much more solidly.

The model relies heavily on pre-trained components (a frozen semantic speech tokenizer from Zeng et al. and a pre-trained ERes2Net speaker model), meaning the high semantic performance is largely inherited from the external tokenizer rather than being an intrinsic capability learned by the codec framework itself.

Training data disparities exist across the compared baselines: SAC is trained on 20,000 hours of multilingual/bilingual speech (including proprietary in-house data), making it difficult to fully isolate architecture improvements from dataset scaling advantages.

strengths: Clear architectural motivation and design: The dual-stream framework explicitly separates linguistic modeling (via a frozen, low-frame-rate semantic tokenizer) from acoustic modeling (via a neural codec), avoiding representation conflict between semantic and acoustic objectives during quantization.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper evaluates both acoustic reconstruction (STOI, PESQ, UTMOS, speaker similarity, and WER) across low- and high-bitrate regimes in clean and noisy conditions, as well as downstream semantic representation quality on the ARCH benchmark.

Strong experimental performance: SAC achieves state-of-the-art results on several key metrics (e.g., WER and UTMOS) at relatively low bitrates, and demonstrates substantial improvements in linear-probing semantic classification tasks compared to existing speech codecs.

Thorough disentanglement analysis: The ablation and masking analyses (semantic-only vs. acoustic-only decoding, SIM, MSIM, and spectrogram visualizations) provide convincing evidence that speaker identity and linguistic semantics are decoupled cleanly.
weaknesses: Incremental conceptual novelty: Decoupling semantic and acoustic features, as well as utilizing pre-trained self-supervised/ASR representations and speaker verification embeddings as auxiliary losses, are established concepts in the speech codec and TTS literature (e.g., SemantiCodec, X-Codec, and related multi-stream tokenizers).

Confounding training advantages: The semantic stream relies directly on a strong, pre-trained frozen speech tokenizer trained on large-scale text-speech datasets, and the codec is trained on ~20,000 hours of curated bilingual data. It is somewhat difficult to isolate whether performance gains stem from the architectural decoupling itself or the superior capacity and training scale of the underlying semantic and speaker teacher models.

Lack of downstream generative evaluation: A core motivation mentioned in the introduction is improving speech language models (SLMs) and zero-shot TTS. However, the empirical validation is restricted to reconstruction and linear probing on ARCH, omitting actual generative experiments (e.g., training an autoregressive SLM or TTS system on the dual tokens to demonstrate practical generative benefits).

Absence of human listening tests: Perceptual acoustic quality is evaluated entirely through automated metrics (UTMOS, PESQ, STOI). Neural vocoders and GAN-based decoders can artificially inflate automatic MOS predictors like UTMOS, making subjective evaluations (e.g., MUSHRA or MOS) desirable for verifying fidelity and naturalness.
